title: Press-Freedom Lawyers Warn of Possible Espionage Act Prosecutions
description_short: At a July 2025 forum, lawyers warned that DOJ’s leak policy could expose journalists to Espionage Act prosecution.
description_medium: At a July 1, 2025, National Press Club event, attorneys Abbe Lowell and Mark Zaid warned that the Justice Department’s revised leak-investigation policy could expose journalists to Espionage Act prosecution. They discussed risks for reporters handling sensitive leaked information; the event concerned a possible legal exposure, not a prosecution already brought.
description_long: Attorneys Abbe Lowell and Mark Zaid used a July 1, 2025, National Press Club event to warn about the effect of Attorney General Pam Bondi’s revised leak-investigation policy on journalists. The event report says the lawyers discussed the possibility that reporters involved in obtaining or publishing sensitive classified material could face Espionage Act prosecution. Discussion connected the administration’s treatment of leak cases with reporters’ ability to protect confidential sources. Their comments described a risk created by the policy and urged reporters to consider that exposure. The event account does not establish that the administration had chosen a reporter for a test case, that a journalist had been prosecuted under the Act, or that the attributed private remark by President Trump was made. Those are separate allegations and require their own sourcing. The documented event is the public warning by two press-freedom lawyers, not evidence of a completed prosecution.

supports: The July 1, 2025 event and warnings by attorneys Abbe Lowell and Mark Zaid about possible Espionage Act exposure for journalists under the revised leak policy.
limits: Does not establish a selected test-case reporter, a completed prosecution, or the attributed private Trump quotation.

title: EPA’s FY2026 Request Proposes a 47% Cut to the Superfund Account
description_short: EPA’s FY2026 request proposes a 47% reduction in the Hazardous Substance Superfund account.
description_medium: EPA’s FY2026 budget justification lists $537.700 million for its FY2025 comparison and requests $282.749 million for the Hazardous Substance Superfund account in FY2026, a proposed $254.951 million decrease (about 47.4%). These are budget-request figures, not enacted appropriations, and they do not show that cleanup at any particular site stopped.
description_long: The EPA’s FY2026 Congressional Justification compares $537.700 million for the Hazardous Substance Superfund account in FY2025 with a $282.749 million request for FY2026. The proposed decrease is $254.951 million, or about 47.4 percent of the comparison amount. The account supports federal hazardous-substance cleanup activity. Because the document is a presidential budget request, the lower figure describes a proposal for Congress to consider, not an enacted appropriation. The table identifies the federal account and its planning figures; it does not show that remediation work at any named Superfund site stopped, nor does it establish cleanup delays or a shortfall in tax receipts. The record should therefore focus on the proposed account reduction and avoid converting the budget request into an outcome claim about sites. The FY2025 comparison is the amount shown in EPA’s document and should be described as its comparison baseline, rather than as a final enacted total.

supports: The FY2025 comparison of $537.700 million, FY2026 request of $282.749 million, and $254.951 million proposed decrease for the Hazardous Substance Superfund account.
The figures are in a budget justification and therefore describe a proposal.
limits: The table does not establish site-level shutdowns or delays, enacted appropriations, or a Superfund tax-receipt shortfall.

title: Bondi DOJ Reverses Limits on Journalists’ Records in Leak Investigations
description_short: Bondi reversed DOJ limits on seeking journalists’ records in leak investigations.
description_medium: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi reversed Biden-era limits on using compulsory process to seek journalists’ records and testimony in leak investigations. Reuters reported that subpoenas and court orders could again be used under the revised policy, which retained procedural safeguards. The change does not by itself establish that reporters were subpoenaed in a later campaign.
description_long: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi reversed a Biden-era Justice Department policy that had sharply restricted compulsory process against journalists in leak investigations. Reuters reported that prosecutors could again use subpoenas and court orders to seek reporters’ records or testimony, subject to DOJ approval. The Justice Manual describes procedural rules for obtaining evidence, including requirements that govern requests involving members of the news media. The reversal changed the department’s approach to protecting confidential sources: a reporter’s records could again be sought as part of a leak investigation under the revised standards. That policy change raised the possibility of greater pressure on journalists and their sources, but it is not evidence that any specific reporter was subpoenaed. The linked material does not substantiate the frozen entry’s claim of an August arrest-and-subpoena campaign. The documented event is the April policy reversal, not a later enforcement action.

supports: Bondi’s April 25 memo reversing Biden-era limits and restoring the possibility of seeking journalists’ records in leak probes.
limits: Reports the policy change; does not document the alleged August 2025 arrests or a broad subpoena campaign.

supports: The DOJ procedural framework for obtaining evidence, including rules governing process directed at members of the news media.
limits: The manual is procedural guidance and does not establish that subpoenas were issued in a specific later case.

title: White House Unveils Privately Funded Rose Garden Renovation Before 2020 Convention
description_short: The White House said private donations funded its 2020 Rose Garden renovation but did not disclose the cost or donors.
description_medium: The White House unveiled a Rose Garden renovation in August 2020, before Melania Trump’s Republican National Convention speech there. Officials said private donations paid for the work but did not disclose the cost or donor identities. The reporting does not support the stored $3.5 million figure or a claim that Republican Party donors funded the project.
description_long: The White House unveiled a renovated Rose Garden in August 2020, shortly before the Republican National Convention. Officials said private donations paid for the work but did not disclose its cost or the donors’ identities. Melania Trump delivered her convention speech from the garden days later, placing the newly renovated space in the setting of a major partisan political event. The timing made the project a subject of public discussion, but the available reporting does not establish that it was undertaken for campaign purposes. It also does not support the stored claim that the renovation cost $3.5 million or that Republican Party donors paid for it. The documented funding description is limited to private donations, with the amount and donor list undisclosed. Keeping those distinctions matters: the renovation and the convention speech occurred in close succession, but that sequence alone does not show who supplied the money or what motive guided the work. The record concerns the renovation and its timing, not a proven campaign-finance violation.

supports: The Rose Garden renovation was unveiled ahead of Melania Trump’s convention speech; officials described private donations as the funding source and did not disclose the cost.
limits: Does not identify donors or establish a $3.5 million cost or campaign purpose.

supports: The timing of the renovated garden and the planned first lady’s speech.
limits: Does not substantiate the stored cost or donor-party affiliation.

supports: The August 22, 2020 White House pool report documenting the garden event.
limits: A pool report does not disclose the renovation cost, donor identities, or campaign motive.

title: Trump Launches U.S. Strikes Against Houthis; Houthi Authorities Report 31 Killed
description_short: The U.S. began strikes against Yemen’s Houthis on March 15; Houthi authorities reported at least 31 killed.
description_medium: On March 15, 2025, the United States began large-scale strikes against Yemen’s Houthis. Reuters reported that Houthi-run health authorities said at least 31 people were killed and 101 injured, mostly women and children. That was an attributed report on the opening strikes, not an independently verified total for the wider campaign.
description_long: The United States began large-scale strikes against Yemen’s Houthi movement on March 15, 2025, in an operation announced by President Donald Trump. Reuters reported that Houthi-run health authorities later gave an early casualty toll of at least 31 people killed and 101 injured, and said most of those casualties were women and children. Those figures are claims attributed to the authorities in territory controlled by the Houthis; they are not an independently verified count. They concern the opening strikes reported that day and should not be presented as a cumulative toll for the entire U.S. campaign. The original entry combined a March 15 start date with a figure of more than 80 deaths that the cited report does not support for that event. The corrected account keeps the start of the operation and the attributed early toll together, while distinguishing a reported figure from independently confirmed casualties. It does not infer civilian status beyond the source’s attribution or claim that the campaign’s total death toll was 31.

supports: The March 15, 2025 launch of large-scale U.S. strikes against the Houthis.
The Houthi-run health ministry’s attributed report of at least 31 killed and 101 injured, mostly women and children.
limits: The casualty figures are attributed to Houthi-run authorities and do not establish an independently verified campaign-wide total or the frozen record’s 80-plus figure.
